inc-incident-lifecycle-severity-metrics.core: Incidents follow a lifecycle: classify severity by impact, detect quickly with symptom alerts (TTD), acknowledge reliably through on-call and escalation (TTA), mitigate first to stop the pain (TTM), then resolve permanently (TTR), measuring each phase to improve.

first_principles.problem: Improvised, unmeasured incident handling prolongs outages and lets them recur.
truths: Each phase has its own bottlenecks.
Mitigation and resolution are different goals.

analogy.title: Emergency medicine
analogy.story: Triage (severity), monitors (detection), the on-call doctor (acknowledge), stabilisation (mitigation), treatment (resolution) and case review (learning).
analogy.breaks: Real incidents loop, with mitigations failing and severity changing, so stay adaptive.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: 14 minutes of customer impact, and no repeat.

check.q: Which phase should be optimised to reduce customer impact time?
check.a: Detection and mitigation (TTD and TTM), since impact ends at mitigation.

inc-command-structure-ic-roles.core: Incident command brings order: a single Incident Commander coordinates and decides (and hands off formally), the Ops Lead and SMEs fix with controlled changes, the Scribe records and the Liaison communicates, all scaled to severity.

first_principles.problem: Without roles, incidents become chaotic, slow and poorly communicated.

analogy.title: An air traffic control tower
analogy.story: One controller coordinates, specialists handle sections, logs record everything and a spokesperson talks to the public.
analogy.breaks: Roles only work if they're practised. Run drills.

example.title: A SEV1 with full command
example.outcome: incidents run like a practised drill.

check.q: What's the single most important role in incident response?
check.a: The Incident Commander, the single source of coordination and decisions.

inc-communication-status-pages-briefings.core: Incident communication controls the narrative: communicate early and on a cadence, run an externally hosted status page as the single source of truth, write plain impact-focused updates with next-update times, brief executives BLUF-style, and notify customers in proportion to impact.

first_principles.problem: Silence or confusing updates create speculation, ticket floods and lost trust.
truths: Information gaps get filled with rumours.
Trust is built through honesty and consistency.

analogy.title: Airline disruption communication
analogy.story: Gate announcements, the departures board, the captain's briefing to operations and SMS only to affected passengers.
analogy.breaks: Legal and security constraints sometimes limit what you can say, so plan those paths in advance.

example.title: A SEV1's communication plan

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Customers and leadership feel informed throughout.

example.outcome: communication that builds trust even during outages.

check.q: What should every public incident update include?
check.a: The user-facing impact, what you're doing, and when the next update will be.

inc-post-incident-analysis-blameless-rca.core: Post-incident analysis turns failure into learning: a blameless culture yields honest data, analysis covers several contributing factors (Swiss cheese) using 5 Whys and fishbone diagrams, and actionable reports with owned, tracked follow-ups change the system.

first_principles.problem: Without structured, blameless learning, incidents repeat and information gets hidden.

analogy.title: Aviation safety investigations
analogy.story: No blame for honest reporting, multi-factor analysis, structured methods and mandatory safety recommendations.
analogy.breaks: Postmortem fatigue is real, so scale the depth to severity.

example.title: A complete postmortem cycle
flow: Shared org-wide; actions tracked to closure

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: The same failure doesn't happen twice.

example.outcome: an organisation that learns from every incident.

check.q: Why focus on contributing factors instead of a single root cause?
check.a: Complex incidents arise from several aligned weaknesses, and fixing several of them gives defence in depth.

inc-disaster-recovery-bcp-rto-rpo.core: Disaster recovery prepares for losing whole sites or regions: the business sets RTO (downtime) and RPO (data loss), strategies run from backup & restore to active-active with matching cost, and only regular failover and restore testing proves the plan works.

first_principles.problem: Without DR, a regional failure or ransomware attack can end the business, and untested DR fails when it's needed.

analogy.title: A city's emergency preparedness
analogy.story: Defined acceptable outage times, backup generators of different sizes, twin hospitals, and regular disaster drills.
analogy.breaks: DR also needs people and process (runbooks, roles), not just infrastructure.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Confidence that the business survives the big one.

check.q: Who should set RTO and RPO targets?
check.a: The business, based on the cost of downtime and data loss, informed by engineering's cost estimates.

inc-complex-systems-theory-safety-ii.core: Complex systems fail through interactions, not broken parts: root cause is a fallacy, organisations drift into failure through normalised deviance, Safety II learns from everyday success, the gap between work-as-imagined and work-as-done reveals hidden risk, and ETTO explains the trade-offs behind 'errors'.

first_principles.problem: Linear, blame-oriented thinking produces shallow fixes and misses how safety is really created.
truths: People adapt to keep systems working.

analogy.title: An ecosystem rather than a machine
analogy.story: Health emerges from countless interactions and adaptations; you nurture resilience rather than replacing a part.
analogy.breaks: Theory needs practical translation into reviews, tooling and culture.

check.q: Name two key ideas from resilience engineering covered here.
check.a: For example, drift into failure (Dekker) and Safety II / ETTO (Hollnagel).

inc-legal-pr-crisis.core: Major incidents are legal and reputational events: know the thresholds that trigger obligations, meet deadlines like GDPR's 72-hour rule, use counsel-directed privileged reporting where needed, apologise with ownership, and sequence communication so the affected hear first.

first_principles.problem: Engineering-only incident handling can create regulatory penalties, litigation exposure and reputational damage.
truths: Trust depends on honesty and order.

analogy.title: Managing a product recall
analogy.story: Regulator deadlines, lawyer-guided investigation, a sincere public statement and contacting affected buyers before the press.
analogy.breaks: Jurisdictions differ, so this is a framework, not legal advice.

example.title: A data breach response
example.outcome: crises managed across engineering, legal and comms.

check.q: What's the first communication step in a major breach?
check.a: Briefing internal leadership, legal and comms so the response is coordinated.

inc-black-swan-engineering.core: Black swan engineering accepts that rare, unpredictable events will happen. Classify your ignorance, treat regions as failure domains, keep the data plane independent of the control plane, design for static stability, break tight coupling to prevent cascades, and practise with game days.

first_principles.problem: Systems built for the failures you've seen collapse under the ones you haven't.
truths: Control planes fail more often than data planes.

analogy.title: Earthquake-resistant buildings
analogy.story: You can't predict the quake, but flexible joints, isolation and drills keep people safe.
analogy.breaks: Robustness costs money, so prioritise the critical paths.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: It survives outages that take down competitors.

check.q: What's the main architectural defence against control-plane outages?
check.a: Static stability: pre-provisioned capacity and cached state so no control-plane actions are needed to keep serving.

inc-resilience-testing-gamedays-ttx.core: Resilience testing exercises both systems and people: live GameDays inject controlled real failures, tabletop exercises rehearse dangerous scenarios verbally across functions, well-designed injections are realistic and ambiguous, and debriefs turn findings into tracked actions and re-tests.

first_principles.problem: Untested people, roles and runbooks fail during real incidents, even with resilient technology.
truths: Some scenarios can only be rehearsed verbally.

analogy.title: Emergency services training
analogy.story: Live drills with real equipment, command-room simulations, realistic scenarios and after-action reviews.
analogy.breaks: Exercise fatigue is real, so keep a sustainable cadence.

example.title: A yearly exercise programme
example.outcome: an organisation that has practised its worst days.

check.q: Why combine GameDays and tabletop exercises?
check.a: GameDays test technical response under real failure, while tabletops rehearse scenarios and decisions that can't be safely simulated.

inc-operational-readiness-prr-capacity.core: Operational readiness gates production: PRRs verify reliability, operations, resilience and change practices, and capacity planning replaces guesswork with forecasting, load testing, queueing maths (Erlang C) and practical rules (N/0.7 headroom, N+1 redundancy).

first_principles.problem: Working code launched without operability or capacity planning fails under real conditions.

analogy.title: Opening a new restaurant location
analogy.story: Inspections (PRR), estimating diners, enough staff so queues don't form, and spare staff for sick days.
analogy.breaks: Readiness is ongoing, so re-review after major changes.

example.title: A new service's launch path
flow: Peak forecast → N=10 → N/0.7=15 → N+1 AZ=18
example.outcome: services that are ready for production on day one.

check.q: Why is simple division insufficient for capacity planning?
check.a: It ignores random arrival bursts and queueing, which cause latency to explode near full utilisation.

inc-runbook-engineering-interactive-docs.core: Runbook engineering reduces cognitive load for stressed responders: alert-linked, consistently structured guides (diagnose with expected output, mitigate, verify, escalate), made executable with pre-filled context, and kept fresh through docs-as-code, ownership, feedback and testing.

first_principles.problem: Tired engineers make slow, error-prone decisions without good, current runbooks.

analogy.title: Aviation checklists and avionics
analogy.story: Clear checklists, increasingly automated cockpit procedures and mandatory updates whenever the aircraft changes.
analogy.breaks: No runbook covers novel failures. Pair them with strong debugging skills.

example.title: A mature runbook system
example.outcome: on-call engineers with a reliable co-pilot.

check.q: What should every alert rule reference?
check.a: A runbook URL describing what it means and how to respond.

inc-on-call-hygiene-compensation-burnout.core: On-call hygiene makes 'you build it, you run it' sustainable: rotations designed for sleep (follow-the-sun, primary/secondary, enough people), fair compensation, measured fatigue with thresholds, and ruthless alert audits so only worthy pages wake anyone.

first_principles.problem: Noisy, unfair, unmeasured on-call burns out the engineers who own production.

analogy.title: A well-run volunteer fire brigade
analogy.story: A fair rota, stipends, tracking call-outs, and fixing faulty alarms so volunteers aren't called out for nothing.
analogy.breaks: Culture matters. Leaders must protect recovery time and prioritise alert work.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Happier engineers and faster real responses.

check.q: What's the single most effective way to reduce on-call burden?
check.a: Auditing alerts so only urgent, actionable, user-impacting issues page a human.

inc-ics-nims-unified-command.core: The FEMA Incident Command System gives tech a proven, scalable framework: command and general staff sections (Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance) mapped to engineering roles, unified command for multi-owner incidents, and span-of-control limits that keep coordination effective as responses grow.

first_principles.problem: Large multi-team or multi-company incidents fall apart without standard structure.

analogy.title: Emergency management for a city-wide disaster
analogy.story: Standard roles, joint command among agencies and manageable teams under each leader.
analogy.breaks: Keep it lightweight. Most incidents need only a few roles.

example.title: A major multi-party outage

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Dozens of responders, coordinated as one.

example.outcome: incidents of any size handled with a proven model.

check.q: What does span of control limit, and why?
check.a: The number of people one lead supervises (about 3–7), because attention and communication break down beyond that.

inc-meta-analysis-organizational-pattern.core: Meta-analysis finds the iceberg: structured incident metadata enables pattern hunting for organisational smells (hotspots, detection gaps, change correlation, repeats, heroes), avoids misleading MTTx means, and is presented to leadership as business impact with concrete investment asks.

first_principles.problem: Treating incidents one at a time misses the systemic causes behind many of them.

analogy.title: Epidemiology for incidents
analogy.story: Code the cases consistently, look for clusters, use the right statistics and brief public-health officials with clear recommendations.
analogy.breaks: Meta-analysis complements, but doesn't replace, deep individual reviews.

example.title: An annual reliability review
flow: Top smell: config changes + customer detection

check.q: What's the prerequisite for incident meta-analysis?
check.a: Consistent, structured metadata captured for every incident.

inc-safety-ii-success-analysis.core: Safety II learns from success: most work goes right because people adapt, so contrast Safety I's 'humans are a liability' with Safety II's 'humans are the source of resilience', study the work-as-imagined/work-as-done gap, and analyse near misses and quiet wins to reinforce protective factors.

first_principles.problem: Learning only from rare failures ignores the abundant evidence of how safety is actually created.

analogy.title: A sports team studying winning plays
analogy.story: Reviewing why plays worked, not just losses, builds a repeatable playbook.
analogy.breaks: Balance it with Safety I, because failures still need rigorous analysis.

example.title: Adding Safety II to an SRE practice
example.outcome: an organisation that learns all the time, not just from outages.

check.a: Situations that went well despite difficulty, which reveal the protective factors worth reinforcing.

inc-sev-definition-matrix.core: A SEV definition matrix objectifies the panic: reach × impact gives a base level, a reference table ties each level to response, communication and postmortem rules, revenue thresholds catch silent business failures, and time sensitivity accounts for escalation and irreversibility.

first_principles.problem: Gut-feel severity causes debates, inconsistent responses and misjudged urgency.
truths: Business impact isn't always technically visible.

analogy.title: A standardised emergency classification system
analogy.story: Like hurricane categories with clear criteria, response protocols, damage estimates and track forecasts.
analogy.breaks: Matrices guide judgement but can't eliminate it, so empower ICs to override with a reason.

example.title: Rolling out a SEV matrix
flow: Draft reach × impact table with examples

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Severity is decided in seconds and consistently.

check.q: Name the three dimensions a sophisticated SEV matrix considers.
check.a: Reach, impact and time sensitivity (often with revenue thresholds as well).
